questions.stem:
The architect for a regional library has received an updated design development estimate of $10,000,000 in today's dollars. The owner's schedule shows construction starting 12 months from now and lasting 12 months. The cost consultant recommends escalating at a simple rate of 4% per year to the midpoint of construction before the estimate is compared with the owner's construction budget.

What escalated cost should the architect report?

options.explanation: This escalates only to the start of construction (12 months).
Correct. The midpoint is 18 months away: $10,000,000 × (1 + 0.04 × 1.5).
This escalates to the end of construction (24 months).
This applies 4% for each of three years.

questions.explanation:
1. Midpoint of construction = 12 + 12 ÷ 2 = 18 months = 1.5 years
2. Escalation = 4% × 1.5 = 6%
3. Escalated cost = $10,000,000 × 1.06 = $10,600,000

questions.stem:
At the end of design development for a medical office building, the architect compares the estimate with the owner's $8,500,000 construction budget. The cost consultant's summary is below. The owner wants to know whether the project is on budget before authorizing construction documents.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Estimated cost of the documented scope | $7,500,000 |
| Design contingency | 10% |
| Escalation to midpoint of construction | 4% |

How does the estimate compare with the budget?

options.explanation: This applies escalation but leaves out the design contingency.
This applies the contingency but leaves out escalation.
This adds the two percentages (14%) instead of applying them in sequence.

questions.stem:
The updated estimate at 50% design development for a 64,000 sf high school addition is 7% over the owner's construction budget. The district has said the budget can't increase, and it wants the gymnasium and science labs kept as programmed. The architect is preparing recommendations for the next owner meeting.

Which recommendations are appropriate? Check the three that apply.

options.text: Reduce area in lower-priority program spaces
options.explanation: Correct. Scope reductions in lower-priority spaces respect the district's priorities.

options.text: Do a value analysis of building systems and materials
options.explanation: Correct. Value analysis finds lower-cost options that still meet performance needs.

options.text: Add deductive alternates to the bid documents
options.explanation: Correct. Alternates let the owner adjust scope based on actual bids.

options.text: Eliminate the design contingency from the estimate
options.explanation: Removing contingency hides risk without lowering cost.

options.text: Proceed with CDs unchanged and rely on bids
options.explanation: Waiting for bids gives up the chance to fix the problem during design.

options.text: Lower the escalation rate to match the budget
options.explanation: Changing assumptions to hit a number doesn't change actual cost.

questions.explanation: §6.5: when the estimate exceeds the budget, recommend changes to size, quality or budget.

questions.stem:
A nonprofit has a total project budget of $12,000,000 for a new community health center, and it asks the architect how much of that is available for construction. Its finance consultant lists the other project costs below. Fees and the owner's contingency are calculated as percentages of the construction cost.

| Project cost | Amount |
|---|---|
| Land | $1,500,000 |
| FF&E | $600,000 |
| Permits and testing | $200,000 |
| Design and consultant fees | 9% of construction |
| Owner's contingency | 5% of construction |

What is the maximum construction cost?

options.explanation: This takes 14% of the $9,700,000 remainder instead of dividing by 1.14.
This leaves out the percentage-based fees and contingency.
This leaves out the land cost.

questions.stem:
Schematic design is complete for an elementary school. The documents include floor plans, building sections, massing studies and an outline narrative of the structural and mechanical systems. No details or specifications exist yet. The school board asks the architect to explain the estimating method, because a board member expects a detailed takeoff.

Which estimating method best suits this phase?

options.explanation: A takeoff needs quantities from detailed documents that don't exist yet.
Assemblies estimates suit DD, once the systems are defined.

options.text: Cost per square foot from comparable schools
options.explanation: Correct. At SD, area-based costs from similar projects fit the information available.
Contractor pricing needs documents that can be priced, and it isn't the architect's estimate.

questions.explanation: SD estimates use area-based (cost/sf) methods. DD uses assemblies. CD uses quantity takeoff.

questions.stem:
The lowest bid for a county recreation center is $6,450,000 against a $6,200,000 construction budget. The bid includes three deductive alternates. The county wants to keep as much scope as possible and accept only the alternates needed to bring the contract within budget.

| Alternate | Deduct |
|---|---|
| 1. Entry canopy | $120,000 |
| 2. Upgraded flooring | $90,000 |
| 3. Photovoltaic array | $180,000 |

Which alternates should the architect recommend accepting?

options.explanation: These deduct $210,000, leaving the bid $40,000 over budget.
Correct. They deduct $270,000, the smallest deduction that brings the bid ($6,180,000) within budget.
These meet the budget but deduct $300,000, more scope than needed.
Deducting $390,000 removes more scope than needed.

questions.stem:
At 95% construction documents for a museum, the owner's finance director asks to remove the design contingency from the estimate, since "design is finished." She also proposes using whatever contingency is left to pay for changes the museum expects to make during construction. Bids are due in six weeks.

Which approach to contingencies should the architect recommend?

options.text: Remove all contingencies once CDs reach 95%
options.explanation: Some design and bidding risk remains until bids are received.

options.text: Keep a small design contingency and a separate construction contingency
options.explanation: Correct. A reduced design contingency covers the remaining document and bid risk. A separate owner's contingency covers changes during construction.

options.text: Use the design contingency to fund construction changes
options.explanation: Mixing the two hides the risk each one covers.
An undifferentiated large contingency doesn't match risk at this stage.

questions.explanation: Design contingency shrinks to a few percent by the end of CDs. The owner's construction contingency is separate.

questions.stem:
On a CMc project for a 90,000 sf office building, the CM's design development estimate is 7% higher than the estimate from the architect's cost consultant. The owner must decide on scope reductions next week and asks the architect to explain the difference so it knows which number to rely on.

Which steps should the architect take? Check the three that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. Quantity differences often explain a large share of the gap.

options.text: Confirm scope assumptions such as allowances and alternates
options.explanation: Correct. The two estimates may price different scope.

options.text: Compare unit prices and escalation assumptions
options.explanation: Correct. Market pricing and escalation dates often differ between estimators.

options.text: Average the two estimates for the owner
options.explanation: Averaging hides the reasons for the difference.

options.text: Adopt the lower estimate to protect the scope
options.explanation: Choosing the convenient number exposes the owner to bid risk.

options.text: Tell the owner the CM's estimate is unreliable
options.explanation: Dismissing it without reconciling is unsupported. The CM prices current market conditions.

questions.explanation: Reconcile estimates line by line: quantities, scope assumptions, unit prices, escalation.

questions.stem:
The schematic design estimate for a 48,000 gross sf office building is $310 per gross sf, or $14,880,000. The owner's construction budget is $14,000,000, and the owner wants to close the gap entirely by reducing area, keeping the same unit cost. The building's gross-to-net ratio is 1.25, and the owner's program lists net assignable areas.

About how many net assignable sf must be removed from the program?

options.explanation: Correct. The gap requires 2,839 gross sf ÷ 1.25 = about 2,270 net sf.
This is the gross area, not the net program area.
This multiplies by the gross-to-net ratio instead of dividing.

flashcards.back: Construction = cost of the work. Project = construction + land, fees, FF&E, permits, financing, owner's contingency.
Includes the contractor's general conditions, overhead and profit. Excludes the architect's fee, land, financing and owner contingencies.
flashcards.confidenceNote: Paragraph number per my knowledge of the AIA document; confirm against your copy (free via your NCARB Record).

flashcards.front: Estimate to compare with the budget
flashcards.back: Scope × (1 + design contingency) × (1 + escalation), applied in sequence.
About 10–15% at SD, shrinking to a few percent at the end of CDs.
SD: cost/sf. DD: systems or assemblies. CD: quantity takeoff × unit prices.

flashcards.front: Max construction cost from a project budget
flashcards.back: (Budget − fixed soft costs) ÷ (1 + percentage-based soft costs).
Recommend adjustments to size, quality or budget: scope cuts, value analysis, alternates, a budget increase.
flashcards.confidenceNote: Paragraph number per my knowledge of the AIA document; confirm against your copy (free via your NCARB Record).

flashcards.back: The smallest combination that closes the gap and keeps the owner's priorities.
Line by line: quantities, scope assumptions, unit prices, escalation. Never just average.

flashcards.front: Area cut to close a cost gap
flashcards.back: Gross sf = gap ÷ $/gsf. Net sf = gross ÷ gross-to-net ratio.
